note.body:
[Let the room settle. Say each word as it lands.]
Same.
(press)
Lesson.
(press)
Same.
(press)
Score.
(press)
When a teacher is observed, their score should mean the same thing whoever observes, however they observe. One coach or another; a coach in the room or a recording on a phone.
This bar is on the form and on the evidence. It is never a bar on a coach. When two honest observers of one lesson disagree, that tells us something useful about the form.
Say it with me. Same lesson. Same score.
(press)
note.first_line: Same.

(press)

cues: press 1: the second quote appears (impact lead, standards and evals)
press 2: "So we decided four things": the four lines
press 3: moves to s06
note.body:
On the planning call on 29 September the worry was this: agreement between coaches, what we call IRR. Does a teacher get the same level whoever observes?
Earlier in September, agreement came out at about 90 in 100, judged too high to be realistic. Most likely, that figure was agreement with Rumi's draft.
(press)
The answer from standards and evals was simple. Coaches capture the evidence; that is their job in the room.
(press)
So we decided four things. Evidence first. A form in two parts. Counts, not ranges. Seventeen rows, with no codes.
(press)
note.first_line: On the planning call on 29 September the worry was this: agreement between coaches, what we call IRR.

note.body:
This is the new form, and it starts blank. Part one runs during the lesson: numbers and a few taps, such as how many children spoke.
(press)
Part two covers independent practice and the wrap-up. Every question describes something the coach can see, in plain words. No indicator names, no codes.
(press)
Before leaving the room the coach picks what the teacher should work on first, and seals the form. From then on, the record is locked.
(press)
Only after the seal does Rumi show what it heard: a quote, the minute, and a yes or no for the coach. Then the coach sees the proposed levels and can change any of them.
(press)
note.first_line: This is the new form, and it starts blank.

[Say: one lesson, two coaches. No school, no names, no day.]
On part 1 of the form, one coach typed that 47 of 53 children spoke; the other, in the same room, typed 20.
Both watched honestly; the gap is about the form, never either coach.

**Two coaches on one lesson reach agreement beyond chance, a kappa of 0.43, where two unrelated lessons give 0.23** (13 pairs, 212 levels). Our bar is 0.40; the range, 0.32 to 0.55, reaches below it: not shown yet.
Exact match 58 in 100 against 49 by chance; within one level, 90 against 81 by chance.
(press)

(press)

(press)
